a: Do not say, "He will notice how many gifts I bring, / and when I make an offering to God Most High, he will accept it."
t: A verse not in MS A
p: MS A has no line for this verse: it goes from 7:8 to 7:15 and then 7:10.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; the Latin (7:11)
readings.orig: μὴ εἴπῃς Τῷ πλήθει τῶν δώρων μου ἐπόψεται, καὶ ἐν τῷ προσενέγκαι με θεῷ ὑψίστῳ προσδέξεται.
readings.en: Do not say, "He will look on the great number of my gifts, and when I offer to God Most High he will accept."
readings.plain: Do not say, "He will notice how many gifts I bring, / and when I make an offering to God Most High, he will accept it."

readings.w: MS A, a medieval Hebrew manuscript from the Cairo Genizah (folio II verso, lines 12-14: no line here, Abegg's transcription)
readings.en: (nothing)

why: The Plain follows the Greek, the base text; the Latin also has the verse.

a: Do not count yourself in with the crowd of sinners;
t: The crowd of sinners, or the leading men?
p: MS A says do not count yourself among the leading men of the people.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: μὴ προσλογίζου σεαυτὸν ἐν πλήθει ἁμαρτωλῶν
readings.en: do not count yourself in the crowd of sinners
readings.plain: Do not count yourself in with the crowd of sinners;

readings.w: MS A, a medieval Hebrew manuscript from the Cairo Genizah (folio II verso, line 18, Abegg's transcription)
readings.en: do not count yourself among the men of the people ("the principle men of the people," Parker and Abegg)
readings.plain: Do not count yourself among the leading men of the people;

why: The Plain follows the Greek. MS A's second line differs too: "Remember that times of trouble will not pass you by" (2v:19, Parker and Abegg), where the Greek has "wrath."

a: the punishment of the ungodly is fire and the worm.
t: Fire and worm, or worms for all?
p: The Greek speaks of the punishment of the ungodly; MS A speaks of the end of every mortal.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; also Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus (which have the plural "punishments"); the Latin (7:19, "ignis et vermis"); KJV
readings.orig: ὅτι ἐκδίκησις ἀσεβοῦς πῦρ καὶ σκώληξ
readings.en: for the punishment of the ungodly is fire and worm
readings.plain: the punishment of the ungodly is fire and the worm.

readings.w: MS A, a medieval Hebrew manuscript from the Cairo Genizah (folio II verso, lines 19-20, Abegg's transcription)
readings.en: for the hope of a mortal is worms
readings.plain: the hope of a mortal is worms.

why: The Plain translates the Greek, the base text of this site, which the churches that count Sirach as Scripture received. MS A gives a reason for humility (everyone ends in the grave), while the Greek gives a warning of punishment.
b: The Greek words recall Isaiah 66:24 and Judith 16:17; see the note on this verse. Swete's notes show that Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus put the line "remember that wrath will not be slow to come" (7:16) after "Bring your soul very low," a change of order only. MS A then has a line the Greek does not: "Do not be hasty to say, 'For a breakthrough, roll yourself upon God and be pleased with his way'" (2v:20, Parker and Abegg).

a: and bend their necks while they are young.
t: Bend their necks, or find them wives?
p: MS A tells a father to find wives for his sons while they are young.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; the Latin ("curva illos a pueritia illorum"); KJV
readings.orig: καὶ κάμψον ἐκ νεότητος τὸν τράχηλον αὐτῶν
readings.en: and bend their neck from youth
readings.plain: and bend their necks while they are young.

readings.w: MS A, a medieval Hebrew manuscript from the Cairo Genizah (folio II verso, lines 25-26, Abegg's transcription)
readings.en: and take wives for them in their youth
readings.plain: and find them wives while they are young.

why: The Plain follows the Greek. MS A's line fits the next verses on daughters and their marriage (7:24-25); the Greek line fits the discipline of the first half of the verse, where MS A also has "discipline them" (2v:25).

a: Do not drive her out.
t: A second line about a wife who is hated
p: The first hand of Codex Sinaiticus, MS A and the Latin add a line warning against trusting a wife one hates.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Alexandrinus
readings.en: do not throw her out
readings.plain: Do not drive her out.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (first hand, after 7:25; a corrector wanted it after 7:26), as Swete's notes give it; MS A (folio II verso, line 28: ושנואה אל תאמן בה); the Latin ("et odibili non credas te"); KJV ("but give not thyself over to a light woman")
readings.orig: και μισουμενω μη εμπιστευσης σεαυτον (Swete's note, unaccented)
readings.en: and do not trust yourself to one who is hated
readings.plain: Do not drive her out. But do not trust yourself to a wife you hate.

why: The Plain follows Vaticanus, Swete's base text, which lacks the line. The line is old, since MS A has it; the Greek copies that lack it may have lost it by accident.
b: The KJV's "a light woman" is its own rendering; the Greek, the Hebrew and the Latin all say "one who is hated" or "a hated woman," which in the Law's language can mean an unloved wife (Deuteronomy 21:15).

a: as you were commanded from the beginning:
t: "From the beginning" or "the first fruits"?
p: One Greek reading says "from the beginning"; another says "first fruits," which the KJV follows.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, first hand (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: as it has been commanded you from the beginning
readings.plain: as you were commanded from the beginning:

readings.w: A corrector of Vaticanus, Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus, which join the word to what follows (Swete's notes); the Latin (7:34) has "sicut mandatum est tibi, primitiarum"; KJV
readings.en: as it has been commanded you: first fruits
readings.plain: as you were commanded: the first fruits,

why: The two readings differ by a few letters (ap' archēs and aparchēn). The Plain keeps Swete's text, which the list still ends with "the first fruits." Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus also add "of holy things" at the end of the verse.

a: the guilt offering, the gift of the shoulders, / the sacrifice of consecration and the first fruits.
t: The priests' share: two lists
p: MS A lists other gifts for the priests than the Greek does.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καὶ περὶ πλημμελίας καὶ δόσιν βραχιόνων καὶ θυσίαν ἁγιασμοῦ καὶ ἀπαρχήν
readings.en: and for the guilt offering, and a gift of shoulders, and a sacrifice of consecration, and first fruits
readings.plain: the guilt offering, the gift of the shoulders, / the sacrifice of consecration and the first fruits.

readings.w: MS A, a medieval Hebrew manuscript from the Cairo Genizah (folio III recto, lines 2-3; some letters of the middle words uncertain, Abegg's transcription)
readings.orig: לחם אבירים ותרומת יד זבחי צדק ותרומת קדש
readings.en: the food of bulls and the heave offering of the hand, sacrifices of righteousness and the holy heave offering
readings.plain: the meat of bulls and the gift from your hand, / sacrifices of righteousness and the holy gift.

why: The Plain follows the Greek. MS A's first words, lechem abbirim, are the phrase of Psalm 78:25, "the bread of the mighty ones"; Parker and Abegg translate them here "the meat of bulls." Abegg's transcription marks several letters of "of the hand" and "sacrifices of" as uncertain.

a: Do not be slow to visit the sick, / for deeds like these will make you loved.
t: Visit the sick, or keep your heart for a friend?
p: MS A has nothing about the sick: it speaks of not turning away from a friend.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; the Latin (7:39)
readings.orig: μὴ ὄκνει ἐπισκέπτεσθαι ἄρρωστον· ἐκ γὰρ τῶν τοιούτων ἀγαπηθήσῃ.
readings.en: do not hesitate to visit a sick person, for by such things you will be loved
readings.plain: Do not be slow to visit the sick, / for deeds like these will make you loved.

readings.w: MS A, a medieval Hebrew manuscript from the Cairo Genizah (folio III recto, line 6, Abegg's transcription)
readings.orig: אל תשא לב מאוהב כי ממנו תאהב
readings.en: do not lift (withdraw) your heart from a friend, for by him you will be loved
readings.plain: Do not turn your heart away from a friend, / for by him you will be loved.

why: The Plain follows the Greek. The two share the second half ("you will be loved") but not the first; Parker and Abegg translate MS A "Do not withdraw your heart from your friend for you will be loved for such things."

a: Do not gloat over anyone who has died;
t: "Your worst enemy"
p: Minuscule 248 and the Latin make it "over your worst enemy who has died," as the KJV has it.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus
readings.en: do not rejoice over a dead man
readings.plain: Do not gloat over anyone who has died;

readings.w: Greek minuscule 248, as Fritzsche's 1871 edition reports it and Hart's edition of 248 prints it ("τῷ ἐχθροτάτῳ σου" added); the Latin ("Noli de mortuo inimico tuo gaudere"); KJV ("thy greatest enemy")
readings.orig: μὴ ἐπίχαιρε ἐπὶ νεκρῷ τῷ ἐχθροτάτῳ σου
readings.en: do not rejoice over the dead man who was your worst enemy
readings.plain: Do not gloat over your worst enemy when he has died;

why: The shorter text of the great codices is the base text. The added words spell out what the line means: the one you would be tempted to gloat over is an enemy.

a: Do not fan the coals of a sinner into flame, / or you may be burned in his blazing fire.
t: Coals, or property?
p: MS A speaks of a wicked man's property, not his coals.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; the Latin (8:13, "Non incendas carbones peccatorum")
readings.orig: μὴ ἔκκαιε ἄνθρακας ἁμαρτωλοῦ, μὴ ἐμπυρισθῇς ἐν πυρὶ φλογὸς αὐτοῦ.
readings.en: do not kindle the coals of a sinner, lest you be burned in the fire of his flame
readings.plain: Do not fan the coals of a sinner into flame, / or you may be burned in his blazing fire.

readings.w: MS A, a medieval Hebrew manuscript from the Cairo Genizah (folio III recto, line 18, Abegg's transcription)
readings.orig: אל תצלח בנחלת רשע פן תבער בשביב אשו
readings.en: do not prosper through the possession of a wicked man, lest you be burned in the flame of his fire
readings.plain: Do not get rich from a wicked man's property, / or you may be burned in the flame of his fire.

why: The Plain follows the Greek. Both have the burning in the second line; the first lines differ: the Greek speaks of coals (anthrakas), MS A of property (nachalat, "possession, inheritance").

a: and do not let anyone pay you back with a favor.
t: A favor paid back, or good things driven away?
p: MS A has a different second line: do not drive good things away from yourself.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: and let him not bring back a favor to you
readings.plain: and do not let anyone pay you back with a favor.

readings.w: MS A, a medieval Hebrew manuscript from the Cairo Genizah (folio III recto, line 27, Abegg's transcription)
readings.en: and do not drive the good away from yourself
readings.plain: and do not drive good things away from yourself.

why: The Plain translates the Greek, the base text. MS A's line is clearer, but it is a different line, not a way of reading the Greek. The Latin (8:22) has a third form: "lest he bring false favor on you." See the note on this verse.

a: Do not let your eyes roam in the city's streets, / and do not wander in its empty places.
t: Roaming eyes, or a fool's eyes?
p: MS A speaks of being made a fool by what your eyes see, and of a ruined house.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; the Latin (9:7)
readings.orig: μὴ περιβλέπου ἐν ῥύμαις πόλεως, καὶ ἐν ταῖς ἐρήμοις αὐτῆς μὴ πλανῶ.
readings.en: do not look around in the streets of a city, and do not wander in its deserted places
readings.plain: Do not let your eyes roam in the city's streets, / and do not wander in its empty places.

readings.w: MS A, a medieval Hebrew manuscript from the Cairo Genizah (folio III verso, line 5, Abegg's transcription)
readings.orig: להתנבל במראה עיניך ולשומם אחר ביתה
readings.en: Your eyes will make a fool of you over a beautiful woman, and your house will become desolate (Parker and Abegg)
readings.plain: Your eyes will make a fool of you over a woman's beauty, / and your house will be left desolate.

why: The Plain follows the Greek. The Greek line is about wandering the streets; MS A's is about the eyes and a ruined house, closer to the warning about beauty in 9:8.

a: and in your spirit you may slide down to ruin.
t: Ruin, or blood?
p: MS A says you will slide "in blood" to the Pit.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καὶ τῷ πνεύματί σου ὀλισθήσῃς εἰς ἀπώλειαν
readings.en: and by your spirit you slip into destruction
readings.plain: and in your spirit you may slide down to ruin.

readings.w: MS A, a medieval Hebrew manuscript from the Cairo Genizah (folio III verso, line 8, Abegg's transcription)
readings.en: and in blood you slide down to the Pit
readings.plain: and in blood you may slide down to the Pit.

why: The Plain follows the Greek. The Hebrew "blood" may be the death penalty for adultery or a husband's revenge; the Greek "spirit" may come from a Hebrew word read differently. See the note on this verse.

a: and on both sides it does wrong.
t: "It does wrong," or "wrongdoing offends"?
p: Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus have a noun, "wrongdoing," where Vaticanus has "wrong things."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: and from both (sides) it will commit wrongs
readings.plain: and on both sides it does wrong.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (first hand) and Alexandrinus (Swete's notes: πλημμεληση, and αδικια in both); Ephraemi has αδικιαν; Fritzsche prints ἀδικία from Alexandrinus, Sinaiticus and many later copies
readings.orig: και εξ αμφοτερων πλημμεληση αδικια (Swete's notes, unaccented)
readings.en: and wrongdoing would offend from both (sides)
readings.plain: and to both of them wrongdoing is an offense.

why: The Plain follows Swete's text. Fritzsche says the Greek ex amphoterōn, "from both," is a faulty translation, and that "against both" was meant. MS A ends the verse "and to both of these, oppression" (folio III verso, line 24, Parker and Abegg).

a: Why are dust and ashes proud?
t: The lover of money
p: Some Greek copies and the Latin add a saying about the lover of money, which the KJV follows.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Ephraemi (Swete's notes)
readings.en: why is earth and ashes proud?
readings.plain: Why are dust and ashes proud?

readings.w: Greek minuscule 106 (before 10:9) and minuscule 248 (after "ashes"), as Fritzsche's 1871 edition reports them; the Latin (10:9-10, "Avaro autem nihil est scelestius... Nihil est iniquius quam amare pecuniam"); KJV
readings.orig: τί ὑπερηφανεύεται γῆ καὶ σποδός; φιλαργύρου μὲν γὰρ οὐδὲν ἀνομώτερον, οὗτος γὰρ καὶ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ψυχὴν ἔκπρακτον ποιεῖ (the addition as Fritzsche prints it)
readings.en: why is earth and ashes proud? For nothing is more lawless than a lover of money, for he makes even his own soul something for sale
readings.plain: Why are dust and ashes proud? Nothing is more lawless than a lover of money, for he puts even his own soul up for sale.

why: The addition is missing from the great codices and from MS A, and it stands in different places in the copies that have it, a sign of a line added from the margin. The Plain follows the base text.

a: Even while he is alive, I have thrown his insides away.
t: "I threw away," "they threw away," or "he threw away"?
p: The copies disagree on who throws away the man's insides.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Swete's notes give no other reading for Sinaiticus (first hand), Alexandrinus or Ephraemi
readings.orig: ὅτι ἐν ζωῇ ἔρριψα τὰ ἐνδόσθια αὐτοῦ
readings.en: because in life I threw away his insides
readings.plain: Even while he is alive, I have thrown his insides away.

readings.w: Greek minuscules 157 and 248, as Fritzsche's 1871 edition reports them; 248 also has "in his life" (ἐν ζωῇ αὐτοῦ), as do minuscule 106 and the Latin
readings.orig: ὅτι ἐν ζωῇ ἔρριψαν τὰ ἐνδόσθια αὐτοῦ
readings.en: because in life they threw away his insides
readings.plain: Even while he is alive, they throw his insides away.

readings.w: The Latin (10:10), of the lover of money; Fritzsche also cites Origen for "he cast away"
readings.orig: quoniam in vita sua projecit intima sua
readings.en: because in his life he has cast away his own insides
readings.plain: Even while he is alive, he throws his own insides away.

why: The Plain keeps the reading of the great codices. A scribe who found "I threw away" puzzling had reason to change it; no scribe had reason to make an easy reading hard. A corrector of Sinaiticus wrote a different line again (Swete's notes).
b: MS A (folio III verso, line 26) has אשר בחייו יורם גויו, which Parker and Abegg translate "that it should lift up its heart during its life," with no verb of throwing. See the note on this verse.

a: A long illness, and the doctor jokes;
t: "Jokes" or "cuts off"?
p: Vaticanus says the doctor jokes; two later copies say he cuts the illness short, as in the KJV.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus; Ephraemi with a spelling slip (Swete's notes)
readings.en: a long illness: the doctor jests
readings.plain: A long illness, and the doctor jokes;

readings.w: Greek minuscules 157 and 248, as Fritzsche's 1871 edition reports them (minuscules 55 and 254 read ἐκκόπτει, "cuts out"); KJV
readings.en: a long illness: the doctor cuts it off
readings.plain: The doctor cuts a long illness short;

why: The two words differ by one letter. "Cuts off" is the easier sense and looks like a correction; the Plain keeps the base text.
b: The Latin has a fuller text with two lines (10:11-12): all power is short-lived, a long sickness weighs on the doctor, and the doctor cuts short a brief sickness. MS A has a different line: "'The smallest illness,' laments the physician" (folio III verso, lines 26-27, Parker and Abegg).

a: For sin is where pride begins,
t: Sin the beginning of pride, or pride the beginning of sin?
p: Vaticanus says sin begins pride; Alexandrinus (first hand), minuscule 248 and the Latin say pride begins sin.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus
readings.en: for the beginning of pride is sin
readings.plain: For sin is where pride begins,

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus, first hand (Swete's notes: ὑπερηφανία and ἁμαρτίας, later corrected); minuscule 248, the Syriac, the Arabic and Chrysostom, as Fritzsche's 1871 edition reports them; the Latin (10:15, "initium omnis peccati est superbia"); KJV
readings.en: for the beginning of sin is pride
readings.plain: For pride is where sin begins,

why: The Plain follows the base text, which MS A supports in sense: it reads "the reservoir of presumption is sin" (folio IV recto, line 1, Parker and Abegg). The reverse form, through the Latin, became the Christian saying "pride is the beginning of all sin"; see the note on this verse.

a: the thrones of rulers
t: Rulers, or proud rulers?
p: The Latin has "proud rulers"; MS A has "the proud."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus
readings.en: thrones of rulers
readings.plain: the thrones of rulers

readings.w: The Latin (10:17, "sedes ducum superborum"); Fritzsche cites the same reading for one other witness
readings.en: thrones of proud rulers
readings.plain: the thrones of proud rulers

readings.w: MS A, a medieval Hebrew manuscript from the Cairo Genizah (folio IV recto, line 3, Abegg's transcription)
readings.en: the throne of the proud
readings.plain: the thrones of the proud

why: The Plain follows the Greek of the great codices. The Latin and MS A both name pride here, the theme of the poem; Thomas Aquinas, reading the Latin, took the line as proof that the chapter speaks of pride as the desire to excel (Summa Theologiae I-II, question 84, article 2).

a: He has withered some of them
t: Withered or removed?
p: Vaticanus says God "dried up" some of the nations; Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and Ephraemi say he "removed" them.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: he dried up (some) of them
readings.plain: He has withered some of them

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Ephraemi (Swete's notes); Fritzsche prints this reading; KJV ("took some of them away")
readings.en: he took away (some) of them
readings.plain: He has removed some of them

why: The words differ by one letter. "Dried up" keeps the plant image of 10:15 (roots and planting), so the Plain keeps the base text; the Latin "arefecit" (10:20) also says "dried up."

a: What race is honored? The human race. / What race is honored? Those who fear the Lord. / What race is despised? The human race. / What race is despised? Those who break the commandments.
t: A different riddle in the longer text
p: The KJV follows a longer Greek text that replaces the riddle with four parallel lines.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus
readings.orig: σπέρμα ἔντιμον ποῖον; σπέρμα ἀνθρώπου· σπέρμα ἔντιμον ποῖον; οἱ φοβούμενοι τὸν κύριον. σπέρμα ἄτιμον ποῖον; σπέρμα ἀνθρώπου· σπέρμα ἄτιμον ποῖον; οἱ παραβαίνοντες ἐντολάς.
readings.en: What seed is honored? Human seed. What seed is honored? Those who fear the Lord. What seed is dishonored? Human seed. What seed is dishonored? Those who transgress commandments.
readings.plain: What race is honored? The human race. / What race is honored? Those who fear the Lord. / What race is despised? The human race. / What race is despised? Those who break the commandments.

readings.w: Greek minuscule 248, in place of the verse, as Fritzsche's 1871 edition reports it and Hart's edition of 248 prints it; KJV
readings.orig: σπέρμα ἀσφαλείας οἱ φοβούμενοι κύριον, καὶ ἔντιμον φύτευμα οἱ ἀγαπῶντες αὐτόν· σπέρμα ἀτιμίας οἱ μὴ προσέχοντες τῷ νόμῳ, σπέρμα πλανήσεως οἱ παραβαίνοντες ἐντολάς
readings.en: A seed of safety, those who fear the Lord; an honored plant, those who love him; a seed of dishonor, those who do not heed the law; a seed of error, those who transgress commandments
readings.plain: Those who fear the Lord are a race kept safe, / and those who love him are an honored planting. / Those who pay no attention to the law are a race without honor, / and those who break the commandments are a race gone astray.

why: The riddle form of the great codices is supported in shape by MS A, which has a shorter riddle (folio IV recto, lines 6-7). The longer text smooths the riddle into plain statements.
b: The Latin (10:23) has a shorter form again: the seed that fears God will be honored, the seed that breaks the Lord's commandments will be dishonored.

a: and those who fear the Lord are honored in his eyes.
t: Those who fear, or he will see?
p: MS A's line is damaged; its letters can be read "one who fears God" or "he will see God."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καὶ οἱ φοβούμενοι Κύριον ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖς αὐτοῦ
readings.en: and those who fear the Lord, in his eyes
readings.plain: and those who fear the Lord are honored in his eyes.

readings.w: MS A, a medieval Hebrew manuscript from the Cairo Genizah (folio IV recto, line 7; the last word partly restored, Abegg's transcription)
readings.en: and one who fears God (or: and he will see God) ... in [his ey]es
readings.plain: and the one who fears God is honored in his eyes.

why: The Plain follows the Greek. The Hebrew letters vyr' can be read "and one who fears," as the Greek has it, or "and he will see," as Parker and Abegg translate ("he will see God with [his ey]es").

a: The fear of the Lord is the first step to being accepted, / but stubbornness and pride are the first step to being thrown out.
t: A damaged line in two later copies, mended by Fritzsche
p: The great codices have no verse 21. Two later copies have a damaged line here; the Plain gives it as Fritzsche mended it.

readings.w: Fritzsche's 1871 edition, in his notes: his own correction ("ego scripsi") of the damaged wording of minuscules 106 and 248
readings.orig: προσλήψεως ἀρχὴ φόβος κυρίου, ἐκβολῆς δὲ ἀρχὴ σκληρυσμὸς καὶ ὑπερηφανία
readings.en: the beginning of acceptance is the fear of the Lord, but the beginning of rejection is hardness and pride
readings.plain: The fear of the Lord is the first step to being accepted, / but stubbornness and pride are the first step to being thrown out.

readings.w: Greek minuscule 106, which Fritzsche says reads προλήψεως in the first word
readings.orig: προλήψεως ἀρχὴ φόβος κυρίου, ἐκβολῆς δὲ ἀρχὴ σκληρυσμὸς καὶ ὑπερηφανία
readings.en: the beginning of anticipation is the fear of the Lord, but the beginning of rejection is hardness and pride
readings.plain: The fear of the Lord is the first step to looking ahead, / but stubbornness and pride are the first step to being thrown out.

readings.w: Greek minuscule 248, as Hart's edition of it prints the line (Fritzsche reports the same wording for 248); KJV
readings.orig: πρὸ λήξεως ἀρχὴ φόβος Κυρίου· ἐκβολὴ δὲ ἀρχῆς σκληρισμὸς καὶ ὑπερηφανία
readings.en: before ending, the beginning is the fear of the Lord; but the throwing out of rule is hardness and pride
readings.plain: The fear of the Lord comes first, before the end, / but stubbornness and pride mean being thrown out of power.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus (no line here; the number 21 is empty in Swete)
readings.en: (nothing)

why: The line is not in the base text. The Plain gives it in square brackets, so that the verse number used by the KJV is not empty, and translates the wording Fritzsche printed. That wording is his own correction of a damaged text: of his first word he writes "προσλήψεως ego scripsi," "I have written προσλήψεως," because 106 has προλήψεως and 248 has πρὸ λήξεως, and he says 248 also has ἐκβολὴ δὲ ἀρχῆς in the second half. So the sense "accepted ... thrown out" is Fritzsche's. The line is not in MS A, which goes from 10:20 to 10:22 (folio IV recto, lines 7-8), or in the Latin.
b: Fritzsche says the line stands after 10:20 in 106 and 248. The KJV's "The fear of the Lord goeth before the obtaining of authority: but roughness and pride is the losing thereof" is close to 248's second half, "the throwing out of rule" (ekbolē archēs).

a: The rich, the honored and the poor:
t: Rich and poor, or sojourner and foreigner?
p: MS A lists the sojourner, the zed (an insolent man, or a scoundrel), the foreigner and the poor.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: rich and honored and poor
readings.plain: The rich, the honored and the poor:

readings.w: MS A, a medieval Hebrew manuscript from the Cairo Genizah (folio IV recto, line 8, Abegg's transcription)
readings.en: sojourner and zed (insolent one), foreigner and poor
readings.plain: The sojourner and the scoundrel, the foreigner and the poor:

why: The Plain follows the Greek. Ephraemi has "the poor and the needy" for "the poor" (Swete's notes).
b: The second Hebrew word, zed, usually means an insolent or arrogant person; Parker and Abegg translate it "scoundrel." Kahana's 1912 edition of the Hebrew prints zar, "stranger," a change of one letter (resh for dalet). MS A goes on, "their glory is the fear of God," with part of the word "fear" restored.

a: will not complain about it.
t: "When he is corrected"
p: Minuscule 248, the Latin and other versions add "when he is corrected," which the KJV has.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus
readings.en: will not grumble
readings.plain: will not complain about it.

readings.w: Greek minuscule 248, as Fritzsche's 1871 edition reports it and Hart's edition of 248 prints it, with the Syriac and the Arabic that Fritzsche cites; the Latin ("non murmurabit correptus"); KJV ("will not grudge when he is reformed")

why: The base text lacks the word. It turns the line from a remark about a free man serving a wise slave into a remark about accepting correction.

a: Many absolute rulers have sat down on the ground,
t: Rulers brought low, or the crushed raised up?
p: MS A has the opposite picture: the downtrodden have sat on thrones.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: many absolute rulers sat on the ground
readings.plain: Many absolute rulers have sat down on the ground,

readings.w: MS A, a medieval Hebrew manuscript from the Cairo Genizah (folio IV recto, line 22, Abegg's transcription)
readings.en: many who were crushed have sat on a throne
readings.plain: Many who were crushed have sat down on a throne,

why: The Plain follows the Greek. Both readings say God reverses fortunes; MS A matches its second line better, where an unexpected person wears the crown.

a: handed over to others
t: Others, or companions?
p: Vaticanus as first written has "companions"; its corrector and the other codices have "others." The Plain follows "others."

readings.w: A corrector of Codex Vaticanus, Alexandrinus, Ephraemi (Swete's notes); the Latin ("in manus alterorum"); KJV
readings.en: into the hands of others
readings.plain: handed over to others

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, first hand, as printed by Swete
readings.en: into the hands of companions
readings.plain: handed over to their companions

why: Swete prints hetairōn, "companions," from the first hand of Vaticanus. By then the vowels ai and e sounded alike, so hetairōn is very likely a spelling slip for heterōn, "others," which a corrector of Vaticanus wrote. MS A says only "were given into the hand" (folio IV recto, line 24). This is a departure from Swete's printed text.

a: Wisdom, knowledge and knowing the law come from the Lord; / love and the ways of good deeds come from him.
t: A verse not in the great codices
p: Vaticanus has no verse 15; later Greek copies, MS A and the Latin have lines here. This verse and 11:16 go together.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus (no line here; the number 15 is empty in Swete)
readings.en: (nothing)

why: The line is not in the base text, so the Plain gives it in square brackets, translated from the Greek of the later copies. MS A has a form of it, so it may go back to Ben Sira himself and have dropped out of the great codices.
b: The Latin is "sapientia, et disciplina, et scientia legis, apud Deum: dilectio, et viæ bonorum, apud ipsum." MS A's chet' where the Greek has "love" is strange in this list; Parker and Abegg translate it "error." The Plain does not follow it.

a: Error and darkness were created along with sinners, / and evil grows old together with those who take pride in evil.
t: A second verse not in the great codices
p: Like 11:15, this verse is not in Vaticanus; later Greek copies, MS A and the Latin have it.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus (no line here)
readings.en: (nothing)

why: As with 11:15, the Plain gives the Greek of the later copies in square brackets.
b: The Latin is "Error et tenebræ peccatoribus concreata sunt..." The line raises a question the book faces in 15:11-20: did God create evil? The verb "created along with" may mean only that error goes with sinners from their beginning.

a: but do not give to the ungodly.
t: The ungodly, or the insolent?
p: MS A has "do not give to the zed," a word for an insolent man, with both letters uncertain.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; the Latin (12:6, "non dederis impio")
readings.en: and do not give to the ungodly
readings.plain: but do not give to the ungodly.

readings.w: MS A, a medieval Hebrew manuscript from the Cairo Genizah (folio V recto, line 6; both letters of the last word marked uncertain, Abegg's transcription)
readings.en: and do not give to the insolent one
readings.plain: but do not give to the proud.

why: The Plain follows the Greek. In MS A this line comes right after the words of 12:7 ("Give to one who is good and withhold from the one who is evil," 5r:5) and reads "Refresh the poor but do not give to the proud" (Parker and Abegg). Kahana's 1912 edition prints zar, "stranger," for zed; the same two words differ at 10:22.

a: A friend is not recognized when times are good, / and an enemy is not hidden when times are bad.
t: "Recognized," "punished," "thrown out" or "thrown in"?
p: Vaticanus has a verb that means "be punished" or "be avenged." The Plain follows "be known," with MS A and the Latin.

readings.orig: οὐκ ἐκβληθήσεται ἐν ἀγαθοῖς ὁ φίλος

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (Swete's notes; Fritzsche reports the same)
readings.en: a friend will not be thrown in, in good times
readings.plain: A friend is not thrown in when times are good, / and an enemy is not hidden when times are bad.

why: This is a departure from Swete's printed text. "Will not be avenged" makes little sense beside "will not be hidden," while "will not be known" matches it exactly. That reading has the support of a corrector of Sinaiticus, MS A and the Latin, so the Plain follows it.
